book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook starts with G-secs and their types (T-bills, dated securities), then pricing, then yield as a formula. Here the video first maps the whole capital market as a tree and walks a road-map down to the government security market, so the learner always knows where the topic sits. Inside, it follows the life of one bond: issued by the government through RBI, first at a discount (zero-coupon), then without a discount, where the learner's objection 'why buy it then?' brings in the coupon. Numbers compare the two kinds side by side. Then the same bond leaves the primary market and changes hands in the secondary market; yield is named only after the first resale is computed, and the inverse rule is drawn last from the story's own numbers.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Follow one government bond through its life (issue, kind, return, resale), and introduce each term only at the step of that life where it is needed.

talmel_summary: Picture and voice land together on 13 of 24 tiles; the picture leads on 9, by 1-5 s, usually as a re-layout or a label that pre-names the next word. The fit is strongest in the bond's life story: the certificate moves from emblem to RBI to the primary market with money going the other way, then steps down a chain of owner boxes carrying its fixed 500 tag while each price and yield sits by its owner, and the same numbers become dots on the yield-price graph; a left road map keeps the learner's place. Weak: the first two minutes are tree labels and definition text that copy the speech, the vivid golden-edge story behind 'gilt-edged' gets no picture, two long paragraph boxes repeat the comparison, and the third resale price (5K) appears only on the graph and is never spoken. No tile falls in the two short transcript losses (386-393 s and about 414-421 s).

voice.notes: About 186 words per minute, calm and conversational, same narrator style as the series ('dekhiye', 'maan ke chalte hain', 'yaani', 'basically'). English finance terms are said in English (face value, discounted price, coupon rate, bond yield). Numbers read in rupees (10,000 rupees, 9,000 rupees, 1 lakh) and percentages plainly (5%, 5.5%, 3.3%). One deliberate suspense cue before the worked example ('bahut dhyan se samjhiye, next 2 minutes mein ek bahut important concept reveal hone wala hai') and one 'important concept' stress on bond yield. The objection 'to koi invest karega hi kyon' is said with a questioning lift. No long pauses.

game_ideas.player_does: Holds a 10-year, 5%, 10,000 face-value bond that pays a fixed 500 a year. News cards arrive (recession, share market boom, better deposit rates); the player decides to buy or sell the bond and at what price in the secondary market.
game_ideas.process_happens: Demand meter moves with the news, buyers bid, the certificate moves to the new owner box, the 500 tag rides along, and the yield = 500 / price is computed and dropped as a dot on the yield-price graph.
game_ideas.win: Predict the direction of price and yield after each news card and end with the highest income on money paid.
game_ideas.lose: Buying at 15,000 in a panic shows the dot landing low on the curve (3.3%) and the rule 'paid more, same 500, lower yield'.
game_ideas.concept: bond yield: fixed 500 coupon, resale at 9K, 15K and a cheaper price gives 5.5%, 3.3%, 10%

game_ideas.player_does: Gets bond cards (face value, price paid, coupon) and drops each through the yes/no gate 'sold at a discount?' into zero-coupon or coupon bond.
game_ideas.process_happens: A timeline runs for each card: the zero-coupon bond pays nothing until maturity and then face value; the coupon bond drops its interest every year and the principal at the end; total return counters fill.
game_ideas.win: All cards sorted and the player can say which pays 500 once and which pays 500 every year.
game_ideas.lose: A coupon bond put in the zero-coupon bin shows its yearly interest coins falling out with nowhere to go, and the gate rule is shown.
game_ideas.concept: coupon rate: why anyone buys a bond without a discount; zero-coupon return

game_ideas.player_does: Plays the government needing money: drags security certificates to RBI, which sells them to banks and NBFCs in the primary market; then one bank sells its bond on in the secondary market.
game_ideas.process_happens: Money flows up to the government as certificates flow down; in the primary market the price is fixed by the government, in the secondary market a demand-supply slider sets it.
game_ideas.win: Raise the target amount and correctly say who sets the price in each market.
game_ideas.lose: Trying to set the secondary-market price as the government is refused with 'here buyers and sellers decide'.
game_ideas.concept: primary vs secondary market; secondary price set by demand and supply

checks_learned: Every input of a spoken result must be spoken or shown at the same moment: a yield of 10% needs its price (5,000) said, not only placed on a later graph.
Every computed percentage in the script must match its arithmetic and one rounding rule (500/9,000 = 5.56%, shown as 5.5%).
A story the narrator tells about a name (golden edges on British bonds) must get a picture in the scene plan; flag 'story with no picture'.
Real bank and company names and logos as characters must be replaced by generic actors (Bank A, Company B).
A teaser line ('important concept in the next 2 minutes') must name the concept, and the scene that pays it off must follow within the stated time.
When two terms differ on one yes/no property (sold at a discount?), the scene plan should use a yes/no fork (worked well here).
Definitions that narrow or redefine a standard term (G-sec only for non-discounted bonds; yield as interest in the secondary market) must be checked against the book source and flagged.
On-screen definition paragraphs over about 25 words should be split into labelled steps or replaced by the picture of the process.
A taxonomy of more than about 8 nodes before the first example should be cut to the path the lesson takes; the rest shown only as a road map.
A promo overlay must never cover a recap screen.

teaching_best.why: The learner's objection ('no discount, so why buy?') is voiced, and the coupon arrives as its answer; the term coupon rate is named only after that, then 'zero coupon' is unpacked as 'no interest'.

One bond with a fixed 500 coupon passes through three owners at three prices, each price change has a story reason (needs liquidity, recession flight to safety, demand falls), and the yield is computed at each step before the term bond yield is defined.
The inverse rule is not stated as a formula first: the story's own numbers become points on the graph, so the rule is read off data the learner has already met.
A yes/no fork ('sold at a discount?') splits zero-coupon bond from bond in one picture.
A left road map keeps the learner's place in the capital-market tree, and its highlight moves to primary and secondary market as the narrator does.

teaching_weak.why: About two minutes of taxonomy (a ten-node tree, shares, bonds, debentures) before any problem or example.

The video narrows 'G-sec' to non-discounted bonds and calls discounted ones zero-coupon bonds of the capital market; doubtful (T-bills are discounted G-secs of the money market). Bond yield is taught only as current yield.
The golden-edge story behind 'gilt-edged' is told with no picture; a memorable image is lost.
Two long paragraph boxes side by side repeat what the narrator says.
The third resale price (5,000) is never spoken; '10%' arrives without its input.
Real bank and company names and logos as buyers.
The recap tree is half hidden by an app promotion; no spoken recap of the bond's life.
